thesis: Erhnam Djinn turned a drawback into deck architecture: a four-mana 4/5 was exceptional so long as the pilot could make the opponent’s granted forestwalk irrelevant.

canonicalIdentity.currentOracleText: At the beginning of your upkeep, target non-Wall creature an opponent controls gains forestwalk until your next upkeep. (It can't be blocked as long as defending player controls a Forest.)

competitiveTimeline.significance: Erhnamgeddon made the card a tournament archetype rather than merely a large creature, and Old School play continues to preserve that relationship between efficient threat and mass land destruction.

playbook.role: Pair the Djinn with land destruction, few or no Forests, and a plan that ends the game before the drawback creates an unblockable attacker. The classic Armageddon pairing converts its size into a post-sweeper clock.

claims.summary: Erhnam Djinn turned a drawback into deck architecture: a four-mana 4/5 was exceptional so long as the pilot could make the opponent’s granted forestwalk irrelevant.
The Djinn triggers during its controller’s upkeep. Granted forestwalk remains after Armageddon, but does not prevent blocking if the defender has no Forest. Factory also dies to Armageddon.
Official results place Lestrée second and Poulter fourth in February 1996; the final paired Erhnamgeddon against Loconto’s control deck.
